title: CR-18 / Module 6 / N6a — Traffic Analysis CTF1
description: Investigate a suspected unauthorized access to a small company's internal web admin panel using nothing but a packet capture taken on the server's internal interface. Recover cleartext credentials from a file transfer service and an unprotected admin panel, assess an obsolete TLS configuration from its handshake alone, and reconstruct the exfiltrated archive from the packets that carried it. Concludes by correlating each finding to the misconfiguration that allowed it.
prerequisites: Working knowledge of TCP/IP: layers, ports, and common application protocols
Familiarity with Wireshark display filters is expected — this lab does not teach them from scratch
outcomes: Perform structured packet analysis using Wireshark and tshark
Identify and extract cleartext credentials transmitted over insecure protocols
Detect weak or misconfigured encryption by inspecting a TLS handshake
Reconstruct files transferred over the network from a packet capture
Correlate observed network data to the underlying security misconfigurations

levels.title: Introduction level
levels.content:
Welcome to the Traffic Analysis lab.

Orion Retail Ltd is a small company with a flat internal LAN. Last Friday the web administrator noticed configuration changes on the internal admin panel that nobody on the IT team made. There is no IDS and no central logging, but a capture was running on the internal interface of the server that hosts both the admin panel and the internal file transfer service.

That capture is all you have. **Your job is to establish how the attacker obtained credentials, what was taken, and which misconfigurations allowed it**.

**The evidence**

* File: `~/case/orion-internal.pcapng` (read-only)
* The server is `172.20.30.10`. The company LAN is `172.20.30.0/24`.
* That network no longer exists. This is an offline review — there is nothing to connect to.

**Before you start**

The attacker was already on the LAN and had placed itself on-path between the admin workstation and the server using ARP poisoning. You can see this yourself in Wireshark under **Analyze -> Expert Information**,  but that’s contextual detail rather than a task — it simply explains how the attacker was able to observe every packet that followed.

Each level gives you a filter to start from. Narrowing it, and working out which of the results actually matter, is the part that is yours. If you get stuck beyond that, each level has hints that will cost you points.

All answers are case-sensitive.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
In the topology panel on the right, right-click **pentester** and select **Open GUI In New Window**. Log in with username **user** and password **password123**.

The capture and a short case brief are in `~/case/`. The `case` shell alias takes you there.

Submit the passkey **start-analysis** to unlock the next level.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been validated for local-only deployment.

levels.title: Credentials In The Clear
levels.content:
Open `~/case/orion-internal.pcapng` in Wireshark. tshark works too.

The attacker was positioned to read traffic between the admin workstation and the server. Two sets of credentials cross the wire in the clear here — one for the web admin panel, one for a service account used by a scheduled backup job.

**Start here.** Apply this display filter to show only the protocols that carry credentials without encryption:

    ftp || http.authorization

The FTP login is plain text. The admin panel uses HTTP Basic authentication, which only base64-encodes the credentials; Wireshark shows the decoded value in the packet detail, or in the `http.authbasic` field.

Note what the service account is used for — you will need it in the final level.

Submit the **password of the service account** as your answer for this stage.
levels.solution:
* Two protocols in this capture carry credentials without encryption. Narrow to them:

```
ftp || http.authorization
```

* **The service account.** The FTP control channel is entirely readable. Right-click any packet in the session and choose **Follow -> TCP Stream** to read the exchange in order, or extract the fields directly using tshark:

```
tshark -r ~/case/orion-internal.pcapng -Y ftp.request.command -T fields -e ftp.request.command -e ftp.request.arg
```

The workstation logs in as `backupsvc` with password `Ba3kup!Or10n#24`, then retrieves `site-backup.zip`. That is the scheduled backup job, and the archive is what you will rebuild in the final level.

* **The admin panel.** It runs on port 8080 with no TLS and uses HTTP Basic authentication, so the credentials are base64-encoded in the `Authorization` header. 

In Wireshark, click one of the two GET /admin/ requests and expand Hypertext Transfer Protocol -> Authorization in the packet detail; Wireshark shows the decoded Credentials: webadmin:Or10n_W3b_2024! beneath the encoded value.

On the command line using tshark, the same decoded field is:

```
tshark -r ~/case/orion-internal.pcapng -Y 'http.authorization' -T fields -e http.authbasic
```

which prints webadmin:Or10n_W3b_2024! once per authenticated request. 

* Both findings are the same class of failure: an administrative interface and a file transfer service, each carrying credentials across the network in a form anyone on-path can read.

**Answer: `Ba3kup!Or10n#24`**

hints.title: That Is Not Encryption
hints.content: The admin panel credentials are base64, not encrypted. Wireshark decodes them into `http.authbasic` — right-click a packet and choose **Follow -> TCP Stream** to read it or decode the Authorization header yourself with `base64 -d`.

levels.title: Encryption That Is Not Protecting Anything
levels.content:
The server has an HTTPS listener on port 8443, and the attacker connected to it. Encryption being present is not the same as encryption being configured correctly.

**Start here.** The client offers a whole list of cipher suites, but only the server's choice describes the session. Filter for the Server Hello:

    tls.handshake.type == 2 && tcp.port == 8443

In the packet details pane, open the TLS handshake and click through the fields to explore what’s being exchanged. Pay attention to the negotiated Version and Cipher Suite — these show what TLS settings the client and server agreed on.

When you expand the certificate, take a moment to look up anything you’re unsure about. A quick search will help you understand the key size, signature algorithm, and validity dates, and each of these counts as a separate finding you should note.

Submit the **cipher suite the server selected**, exactly as Wireshark names it, without the hexadecimal value in brackets.
levels.solution:
* Find the TLS traffic. The listener is on port 8443. The Client Hello (`tls.handshake.type == 1`) advertises a long list including modern AES-GCM suites — that list is irrelevant, because the server picks. Filter for the Server Hello:

```
tls.handshake.type == 2 && tcp.port == 8443
```

This selects one packet (frame 342). Click it, and in the packet detail pane expand Transport Layer Security. Right-click that line and choose Expand Subtrees to open the whole thing at once.

The tree is:
```
Transport Layer Security
  TLSv1 Record Layer: Handshake Protocol: Multiple Handshake Messages
      Version: TLS 1.0 (0x0301)
      Handshake Protocol: Server Hello
          Version: TLS 1.0 (0x0301)
          Cipher Suite: TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA (0x0005)
          Compression Method: null (0)
      Handshake Protocol: Certificate
      Handshake Protocol: Server Hello Done
```

The record layer is labelled Multiple Handshake Messages because the server packed its whole reply — Server Hello, Certificate and Server Hello Done — into one record. The two lines that answer this level sit under Handshake Protocol: Server Hello:

* Version: TLS 1.0 (0x0301) — deprecated by RFC 8996 and removed from every current browser.
* Cipher Suite: TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA (0x0005) — RC4 is a broken stream cipher prohibited by RFC 7465, the RSA key exchange gives no forward secrecy, and integrity rests on SHA-1.
* On the command line the same two values are:

```
tshark -r ~/case/orion-internal.pcapng -Y 'tls.handshake.type==2' -T fields -e tls.handshake.version -e tls.handshake.ciphersuite
```
* The certificate is the sibling node Handshake Protocol: Certificate in the same packet. Expand it down through Certificates -> Certificate -> signedCertificate and note it is self-signed (issuer and subject both srv-web01.orion.local), uses a 1024-bit RSA key (subjectPublicKeyInfo -> publicExponent 65537, modulus 1024-bit), is signed with sha1WithRSAEncryption, and its validity ran 2019-03-14 to 2020-03-13 — expired. Nothing here needs decrypting: version, cipher suite and certificate all travel in cleartext during the handshake, and the configuration itself is the finding.
* Submit the cipher suite name without the hexadecimal value.

**Answer: TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA**

hints.title: Client Offers, Server Decides
hints.content: In a TLS handshake the client sends a list of cipher suites it supports (Client Hello, tls.handshake.type == 1); the server replies with the single one it chose (Server Hello, tls.handshake.type == 2). Only the server's choice describes the session — so look at the Server Hello, not the Client Hello, and read the Cipher Suite line inside it.

levels.title: Rebuild What Left The Building
levels.content:
A capture contains the files that crossed the network, not just a record that they moved. The archive the backup job transferred can therefore be rebuilt from the evidence you already have.

**Start here.** Let Wireshark carve it out for you: **File -> Export Objects -> FTP-DATA**, select `site-backup.zip`, and Save As into your home directory. (On the command line: `tshark -r ~/case/orion-internal.pcapng --export-objects ftp-data,~/out -q`.)

The archive is encrypted, but do not try to crack it — you already recovered the password earlier in this lab. Open it, read the notes inside to understand how this happened, and find the flag.

Submit the **flag contained in the archive** as your answer for this stage.
levels.solution:
* **Locate the transfer.** The FTP control channel negotiates a separate connection for the file itself: the `227` response to `PASV` gives the address and port (`172,20,30,10,197,42` = port 50474), and `RETR site-backup.zip` names the file. Because Wireshark parses the control channel, it recognises the data connection automatically and labels it `ftp-data`.

* **Carve out the file.** In the GUI: **File -> Export Objects -> FTP-DATA**, select `site-backup.zip`, then Save As into your home directory. On the command line:

```
mkdir -p ~/out
tshark -r ~/case/orion-internal.pcapng --export-objects ftp-data,~/out -q
```

* **Open it** with the service account password recovered earlier:

```
unzip -P 'Ba3kup!Or10n#24' ~/out/site-backup.zip -d ~/out/backup
cat ~/out/backup/flag.txt
```

* **Why that worked** is the point of the level. `notes.txt` states it plainly: the archive password was deliberately set to match the backup service account so staff would not have to look it up. A single cleartext FTP session therefore yielded both the archive and the means to open it. `config.php` compounds the problem — the same credentials appear again in source, with `FORCE_HTTPS` disabled.

* End to end: no ARP protections on a flat network let the attacker sit on-path; cleartext FTP and HTTP Basic handed over credentials; password reuse turned a stolen encrypted archive into a readable one. None of it required an exploit.

**Answer: `ORION{p14nt3xt_ftp_l34ks_3v3ryth1ng}`**

hints.title: You Already Have The Password
hints.content: The archive password is one you recovered in an earlier level — somebody reused it. `unzip -P '<password>' site-backup.zip`.

levels.title: Lab Completed
levels.content:
You've completed the Traffic Analysis lab.

From a single packet capture and no logs, you recovered two sets of credentials from protocols that should never have carried them, assessed a TLS configuration from its handshake alone without decrypting anything, and reconstructed a transferred file from the packets that carried it.

Every technical finding reduces to a configuration choice somebody made and nobody revisited: an admin panel without TLS, a backup job over cleartext FTP, a 2019 TLS configuration left in place, a flat network with no ARP protections, and an archive password reused from a service account.


**Findings and fixes**

* Flat network, no Layer 2 protection. ARP poisoning let the attacker sit between the workstation and the server and read their traffic. Fix: dynamic ARP inspection, port security, network segmentation.
* Admin panel over plain HTTP (port 8080). HTTP Basic auth only base64-encodes credentials, exposing webadmin on the wire. Fix: enforce TLS, disable the plaintext listener.
Cleartext FTP for the backup job. The backupsvc account crossed the network in full view. Fix: replace with FTPS or SFTP.
* Obsolete TLS on port 8443. TLS 1.0 with TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA, no forward secrecy, behind a self-signed 1024-bit SHA-1 certificate expired since 2020. Fix: TLS 1.2+, modern cipher suites, a valid certificate.
* Password reuse. The archive was locked with the same password as the FTP service account, so one intercepted login opened the stolen file. Fix: unique credentials per service, a secrets manager, no shared passwords.

The throughline: no exploit was used. Each finding is a configuration choice; the password reuse is what turned interception into full compromise.
